questions.q: In Part A, what does the addPassword event on meridian-reporting-sp's application registration reveal?
options: The attacker's persistence step -- a second credential added so rotating the original secret alone won't remove their access
That the service principal was deleted entirely
A routine, scheduled credential rotation performed by Meridian's own automation
That Conditional Access blocked the sign-in automatically
questions.explain: addPassword matches Lesson 25's persistence stage -- the attacker adding their own credential to the identity they already compromised.

questions.q: Why does containment in Part A set accountEnabled to false on the enterprise application rather than just rotating the one known-leaked secret?
options: Rotating a secret is not possible on Azure service principals
accountEnabled only affects human user accounts, not service principals
Disabling sign-in blocks every credential tied to the app at once -- old and newly added -- without waiting for the full secret list to be reviewed
accountEnabled must be set to false before any Activity Log query can run
questions.explain: Disabling sign-in immediately blocks all credentials on the app, including any the attacker added, which rotating a single known secret would not.

questions.q: In Part B, what does the CreateAccessKey event on meridian-sync-user represent?
options: A failed login attempt
The persistence step -- a second, attacker-created access key existing independently of whichever key actually leaked
Confirmation that the IAM user was deleted
A routine AWS key-rotation reminder email
questions.explain: CreateAccessKey on an already-compromised IAM user is the same persistence pattern from Lesson 25 -- T1098.001 -- seen on the AWS side.

questions.q: Why does the lab deactivate both of meridian-sync-user's access keys with update-access-key --status Inactive rather than deleting them immediately?
options: AWS does not allow IAM access keys to be deleted under any circumstance
Deleting a key requires disabling the entire AWS account first
Inactive keys continue to function normally for read-only calls
Deactivating immediately blocks use of both keys while preserving them as evidence for the investigation, rather than destroying them outright
questions.explain: Setting a key to Inactive blocks it from being used right away without destroying it, which keeps it available for the investigation before a later deletion.

questions.q: Why does containment happen within minutes of detection in both Part A and Part B, before every log entry has been fully reviewed?
options: Cloud providers require containment within a fixed SLA window or they revoke the account automatically
A full investigation is not actually necessary once containment is complete
Waiting for complete certainty lets a still-active compromised identity keep making calls -- each additional minute is another possible enumeration, persistence, or abuse action
Containment actions cannot be reversed, so investigators wait for certainty in every other case except this one
questions.explain: Lesson 28 established that containment shouldn't wait for full certainty, since every extra minute lets a still-compromised identity act again.
